title: Quantum Alliance forms amid warnings 6.4 million bitcoin face future quantum threat
key_facts: Nine crypto companies unveiled the Quantum Alliance on Thursday (15 Oct 2026) to develop common security standards for bitcoin, Ethereum and other blockchain networks.
Members include Hacken, Midnight Foundation, Quantus and Postquant Labs; the alliance plans to publish common security tests and guidance for moving existing networks to quantum-resistant systems.
The concern is that future quantum computers could work out a wallet's secret key from its publicly visible key and steal the funds.

The alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin, or 30.2% of the supply, have public keys already exposed; those coins cannot be stolen this way today because no existing quantum computer is powerful enough.

Richard Carback, chief technology officer of Postquant Labs, believes 2028 is a realistic date for a machine that can break today's cryptography; Bryn Bennett, chief revenue officer at The Vault, says nobody knows the date.
Christopher Smith, CEO of quantum-resistant blockchain Quantus, says whoever gets the first cryptographically relevant quantum computer will probably take Satoshi Nakamoto's 1.1 million bitcoin.
Experts differ on freezing vulnerable coins: Carback prefers moving them, Bennett calls a freeze a governance decision for the Bitcoin network that would set a precedent on property rights.

Making bitcoin quantum-resistant means replacing its digital signatures, which needs agreement among developers, miners, wallet providers, exchanges and users, and the new signatures could take more space and raise fees.

why_it_matters_hint: A large share of bitcoin sits at addresses with exposed public keys, and the fix needs wide agreement among the people who run the network.
